New Baseball America top 10 prospects list shows depth and versatility changes in Red Sox system

ByHunter Noll|Nov 24, 2026, 6:43 PM EST
Add us as a preferred source
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:15
Instaread

Baseball America has released its latest prospect rankings, including its top 10 prospects in the Boston Red Sox system.

No one will be surprised by the first few names. However, when you get deeper into the top 10, a few things start to become noticeable.

We have seen some high highs and some low lows when it comes to the Red Sox's farm system over the years. There was the “Big Four,” but there was also a time when we were trying to convince ourselves that a barren system wasn’t exactly that.

Alex Speier dropped his top 10 prospect list for Baseball America, and it highlights a few key things (subscription required).

Franklin Arias, Justin Gonzales, Franklin Primera and Sadbiel Delzine are a ridiculous first four. Arias has a case to be called the best prospect in baseball. Meanwhile, Gonzales has limitless power potential, a good hit tool, and a plus-plus arm. Primera is an all-around great catcher. Finally, Delzine has the early looks of an ace prospect. 

Baseball America’s top 10 prospect list for the Boston Red Sox highlights a lack of variety and depth in the system

I’d add Juan Valera to that group because when he’s on the mound, he’s phenomenal. However, he hasn’t been healthy enough for me to put him in that elite group.

Henry Godbout has a realistic chance to become a top 100 prospect this year. Owen Hull looks like he’s going to fly through the minor leagues. Jake Schaffner has a strong hit tool with great defense and elite speed. Dylan Brown had a big 2026, and John Holobetz has been fantastic since arriving in the organization in 2025.

So what are the issues? The first is variety. In that top 10, there are four starters (three righties), three shortstops, two outfielders and one catcher. You might feel like that’s not a fair representation of the entire farm system, but it does point to a problem they have. The Red Sox fixed the catching depth last offseason.

They have very little in terms of first base prospects, though. Gonzales plays there very sparingly. Besides him, it’s basically Brooks Brannon and Antonio Anderson.

At third base, they have Mikey Romero, but the team hasn’t seemed super invested in him. The Red Sox also have Jack Winnay, Louis Andujar and Anderson in their hot corner mix.

Meanwhile, in a stark contrast to their major league starting rotation, the Red Sox are extremely right-handed when it comes to pitching prospects.

Obviously, things change quickly in baseball. Trades happen, you make additions through free agency and drafts, players grow, and then we might be talking about this situation entirely differently in July. Right now, the Red Sox have a few obvious areas of need.

The other issue is depth. Boston sees a pretty hard drop-off as you start to move down the list. I’m a fan of Dylan Brown, but he’s a college pitcher who put up strong numbers in Single-A and High-A last season. John Holobetz is awesome, but he’s a back-end rotation or bullpen arm. They're weaker No. 9 and 10 prospects than the Sox had a few seasons ago.

Believe me, these are far better prospects than what the Red Sox had in the dark days. And some teams are still in worse situations. However, there is a clear drop-off as you go further down the list.

It’s not the end of the world. Again, Boston could be in a worse spot. But the lack of depth means there are very few bullets if it wants to make a big trade. If the Red Sox want to make some big splashes on the trade market, they’re severely limited in their options for who to trade from at the moment.

This is a moving situation. In a few months, we might be looking at the farm system in a completely different light. The Red Sox have enough top-end talent and more than enough intriguing prospects who could take a step forward that it wouldn’t be shocking if they are considered a top system again soon. For now, though, variety and depth are issues that need to be addressed to get the farm system rolling again.
